Dear editor-in-chief,

We would like to resubmit our article "Speak less, say more. Finding the preconditions for the reducing effect with an agent-based model" to the Language and Cognition journal. We believe our article remains an interesting contribution to the journal: we show that, in our agent-based simulation, the "simple" reducing effect nonetheless requires elaborate cognitive underpinnings in order to guarantee a stable communication system. Both our theoretical model as well as our simulation *and* our findings are now also more explicitly rooted in the reception/production literature. The best example of this is our complete reworking of the model architecture, which is now Bayesian, as in the @kleinschmidt_robust_2015 speech perception model.

Still, we would like to stress that our computer simulations *can* be informative about communication as a whole. The fact that we do not simulate rich linguistic structures is the crux of our simulations: we want to forego the self-evident mechanisms found in real life to focus on the basics of mechanisms such as the reducing effect. Later, when we understand how the basics work, we can expand upon this knowledge. We believe frequency should also be understood as linguistic context, as it exists outside of the acoustic signal itself and is informative to the hearer to make an interpretation of that acoustic signal. This idea is now also the starting point of our article, i.e. whether this frequency information, which we can now explicitly disable in our Bayesian perception model, is enough to keep communication stable in ambiguous circumstances. We then further build upon our findings to look into more cognitively elaborate ambiguity avoidance mechanisms.

Furthermore, we want to stress that our visual analysis follows the standard procedure in agent-based simulation research. While experimental studies rely on inferential statistics to generalise from limited datasets, computer simulations can approximate infinite trials to exhaustively explore a parameter search space [@ohmer_communication_2025]. In this sense, a concept like "significance" loses its meaning, and this is also why we do not inferential statistics to interpret our results. We have, however, condensed the most important comparisons in much better graphs which expicitly compare model behaviour across different parameters. This should make the differences in behaviour between these models more clear.

Our article has further been improved in several ways: we implemented another ambiguity avoidance mechanism from speech perception literature [@todd_word_2019], simplified the frequency distribution variations, updated our reduction mechanism, addressed the role of meaning, and improved the overall structure of the article. We have fewer model variations, less repetition and, in general, a much more readable paper.

We are convinced that our contribution can help researchers become more aware that seemingly simple phenomena, such as the reducing effect, might be more cognitively involved when actually implemented. This is, again, why we think our work remains relevant for Language and Cognition.

Many thanks in advance,  
Anthe Sevenants, Freek Van de Velde and Dirk Speelman
